summaries.example: Imagine a weather map. The map is not the sky, and it does not copy every cloud. Still, its colors and symbols can help you figure out where rain may fall. Scientists use models in a similar way. A model may leave things out or make them simpler, but it can still help people reason about a real target.
summaries.summary: Scientific representation is the study of how science uses things such as maps, pictures, graphs, equations, and models to tell us about the world. Philosophers do not all agree on one answer. Some say representation comes from similarity, some emphasize matching structures, and others focus on how people use models to draw conclusions. Another view compares models with stories or games of make-believe, while representation-as views ask what a model presents its target as being. The central lesson is that a scientific representation is not simply a mirror image. It may be idealized or partly wrong and still help us investigate its target. Philosophers therefore ask several connected questions: what makes something a representation, how does it point to a target, how can we judge accuracy, what kinds of styles exist, what are models made of, and how can mathematics help describe physical systems?
key_ideas: Science uses many kinds of representations, including pictures, measurements, graphs, equations, and models.
A representation does not have to be a perfect copy. A useful model may simplify, change, or leave out features.
Philosophers ask what makes something a representation and how it helps us learn about its target.
A good account must explain how models support reasoning, how inaccurate models can still represent, and how models without real targets can work.
Representations can work in different styles, and their success depends partly on what they are being used for.
summaries.why_it_matters: We learn much of science through representations rather than by looking directly at everything. We cannot see an atom with our eyes, hold a climate in our hands, or place an entire economy on a desk. Models and other representations help scientists ask questions and make comparisons. Understanding their strengths and limits can help us use scientific pictures, charts, and models more carefully.

important_terms.definition: A picture, map, number, model, or other thing used to tell us about something else.
The real thing, part of the world, or idea that a representation is about.
A simplified tool scientists use to study a target, such as a map, diagram, equation, or pretend system.
Using a model as a stand-in so that thinking about the model can help us form ideas about the target.
A representation that gets something wrong while still being a representation.
The way a representation points toward its target, rather than the target pointing toward the representation.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be useful for learning even if it is not an exact copy?
What makes a map different from a random drawing that happens to look similar?
Can a story about an imaginary creature teach us something about real animals?
Why might two models of the same thing be useful in different ways?

summaries.example: Consider a model of a population that treats all organisms as identical and assumes reproduction happens at regular intervals. It may not accurately describe every individual or every event. Yet researchers can use the model to derive consequences and compare them with a real population. Its simplifying assumptions may be part of its modelling style rather than a reason to reject it altogether. The philosophical question is what connects the model to the population and justifies moving from results about the model to claims about the target.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of scientific representation asks how scientific models and other representational devices enable inquiry into the world. The entry argues that there is not one simple problem but a cluster of issues. An account must explain what establishes a model-target relationship, how that relationship is directed, how reasoning about a model can yield hypotheses about its target, how inaccurate models remain representations, how models about nonexistent systems can function, how different representational styles are classified, what models are, and how mathematics connects with physical systems. Several approaches are assessed. Similarity-based theories appeal to shared features but face problems involving symmetry, reflexivity, excessive inclusiveness, idealization, and nonexistent targets. Structural theories appeal to formal mappings, yet exact mappings can exclude distortive models and do not by themselves select a target. Inferential theories make model-guided reasoning fundamental, though they must explain what makes such inferences justified. Fiction and representation-as theories offer alternative accounts involving imaginative description, denotation, exemplification, interpretation, and imputed properties. The debate remains open, and the approaches may answer different parts of the overall problem.
key_ideas: The entry separates several problems: what representation is, how scientific representation is distinguished, which styles exist, how accuracy is judged, and what models are.
Any account must explain surrogative reasoning, misrepresentation, targetless models, directionality, and the application of mathematics.
Similarity is attractive because it seems to explain why model results can inform us about targets, but similarity alone is symmetric, reflexive, and too inclusive.
Structural accounts use mappings such as isomorphism or homomorphism. These can explain formal relationships, but exact structural matching has difficulty with idealization and misrepresentation.
Inferential accounts make the reasoning from model to target central. They differ over whether that reasoning can be explained without relying on a prior representational relation.
Fictional and representation-as approaches emphasize imagination, interpretation, denotation, exemplification, and what a model presents a target as being.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scientific conclusions often depend on models that simplify, idealize, mathematize, or even describe systems that do not exist. A model's usefulness therefore cannot be measured only by whether it copies its target. The debate clarifies how scientists move from equations, simulations, diagrams, or material models to claims about nature. It also helps identify when a model is informative, what its limitations are, and why different models can represent the same system in different ways.

important_terms.definition: The broad philosophical problem of explaining what makes a scientific model represent a target system.
The wider problem of explaining representations that support reasoning about a target, whether or not they are specifically scientific.
Reasoning performed on a representation that is used to form hypotheses or conclusions about its target.
The question of how scientific representations differ from other representations that also support reasoning.
A pattern or manner in which a model represents, such as emphasizing causal, structural, or other features.
Criteria for deciding whether a representation succeeds in showing its target in the relevant respects and degree.
The question of what sort of entities models are, including physical objects, structures, descriptions, or other items.
A relation or mapping that preserves some structure between a model and a target or between structures associated with them.

questions_to_think_about: If two objects are similar, why does one represent the other rather than the reverse?
Can an inaccurate model still count as a representation? What would make it inaccurate rather than merely irrelevant?
Does a model need an actual target in order to represent something?
Are mathematical structures enough to explain how mathematics applies to physical systems?
Should there be one general theory of representation, or should different representational styles receive different explanations?

summaries.example: Suppose a school uses a floor plan to plan an evacuation. The plan may enlarge hallways, leave out decorations, and use arrows that are not part of the building. Even so, students can reason from it about routes. A map also needs a key: a symbol or color must be connected with what it stands for. This shows why representation is more than looking alike. The plan is useful because people interpret it for a purpose and use it to draw conclusions about the real building.
summaries.summary: Scientific representation concerns the many tools scientists use to learn about things they cannot study simply by looking at them directly. These tools include images, graphs, measurements, equations, theories, and models. The philosophical debate begins with several questions rather than one: what makes something represent a target, how does it support reasoning, how do we tell scientific representation from other representation, what styles are possible, how do we judge accuracy, and what are models? One proposal says models represent because they resemble their targets, but resemblance is not enough: similar things do not automatically represent one another, and a representation can be inaccurate. Another proposal uses mathematical structures and mappings, but exact matching can have trouble with idealized models. Other proposals focus on the intentions and interpretations of users, on the inferences models permit, on models as imaginative descriptions, or on what models present their targets as being. The entry treats these as competing approaches to connected problems. It emphasizes that models need not be copies and that their usefulness depends on how they are used for particular purposes.
key_ideas: Scientific representations include measurements, photographs, diagrams, maps, equations, theories, and models.
Philosophers disagree about whether representation is based mainly on similarity, formal structure, user intentions, inference, imagination, or properties presented by a model.
Similarity alone cannot explain representation: many things resemble each other without one representing the other.
A representation can be wrong and still represent. This is why theories must allow misrepresentation.
Some models concern nonexistent systems, such as idealized systems or proposed entities. A theory must explain how these models can still be used.
Representations point from the model or image to the target. This one-way feature is called directionality.
summaries.why_it_matters: Models influence how people understand scientific claims. A diagram can make a process visible, an equation can reveal relationships, and a simulation can let researchers explore possibilities. But every representation selects some features and leaves out others. Learning how representation works helps us ask what a model actually shows, what it assumes, and whether its conclusions apply to the real target.

important_terms.definition: Something used to provide information about another thing, such as a map, graph, image, equation, or model.
The part of the world or subject that a representation is about.
A simplified scientific tool used to investigate a target system.
Using a representation as a stand-in for reasoning about the target it concerns.
The problem of explaining how scientific representations differ from non-scientific ones.
The manner in which a model highlights or organizes features of its target.
A way of deciding whether a representation gets its target right in the respects that matter.
A formal relationship between structures that preserves selected relations.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a floor plan not required to look exactly like a building?
Can a model be helpful even when some of its assumptions are false?
What makes a scientific model different from a random object that happens to resemble its target?
How might the user's purpose change which features count as important?
Why could two models represent one target in different styles?
